prompt: In the spreadsheet example, Organic grew 60.0% and Paid shrank 26.67% from week 1 to week 8. A naive unweighted average of those two percentages is +16.67%, suggesting healthy overall growth, but the real combined signups fell 12.22% over the same period. What explains the gap?
choices: The unweighted average contains an arithmetic error; recomputed correctly it also equals -12.22%

Paid started out with far more signups than Organic (150 vs. 30 in week 1), so its decline should count for much more than Organic's growth when weighted by volume -- exactly what a volume-weighted average does
Percent changes can never be averaged together under any circumstances
The -12.22% figure must be a typo, since both calculations should always give the same number

prompt: A startup's dashboard currently shows total signups since launch, total page views since launch, and total social-media followers. A teammate proposes replacing it with a single chart: week-over-week activation rate. What's the strongest argument for the change?
choices: The vanity metrics are mathematically incorrect and need to be recalculated

Cumulative totals almost always climb regardless of whether the business is healthy, so they never prompt a different decision, while a week-over-week rate can actually fall and trigger an investigation -- like the drop from 30.0% to about 20.9% even as signups rose 30%
Dashboards should never display more than one number, as a general design rule
This is the same kind of dashboard DevOps teaches for monitoring server uptime and latency, just applied to a product instead of infrastructure

A two-proportion z-test on an A/B test (Blue: 160/2000 = 8%, Green: 200/2000 = 10%) gives z ≈ 2.21. Using the conventional two-tailed threshold of 1.96 for 95% confidence, what should you conclude?
choices: The result is not significant, since 2.21 is only slightly bigger than 1.96
The result is significant -- 2.21 clears the 1.96 threshold, so the 2-percentage-point gap is unlikely to be due to chance alone at the 95% confidence level
A z-test cannot be applied to conversion-rate data; only a t-test can

prompt: A team runs an A/B test and checks the result every day, stopping the moment the p-value first dips below 0.05, instead of waiting for the pre-planned sample size. Which specific pitfall is this, and why is it a problem?
choices: Survivorship bias -- they're only looking at the users who survived to see the result

Peeking -- repeatedly checking a test and stopping as soon as it looks significant inflates the real false-positive rate well above the nominal 5%, since chance gets many separate opportunities to cross the threshold
Multiple comparisons -- they are comparing more than two groups against each other at once
This isn't actually a problem, since each individual day's p-value is computed correctly on its own

prompt: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents are strongly correlated (r ≈ 0.998 in this lesson's worked numbers). What's the correct conclusion?
choices: Eating ice cream causes an increased urge to swim in unsafe conditions

Both variables are driven by a shared confounding variable -- summer heat -- which independently increases ice cream buying and swimming (and therefore drowning risk); there is no direct causal link between the two
The correlation must be a statistical fluke, since ice cream and drowning have no plausible connection
Drowning incidents cause ice cream sales to rise afterward, as a form of comfort spending
